title: Toy Models of Superposition
hook: Why is a single neuron so hard to interpret? It may be doing several jobs at once. Networks pack more features than they have neurons by overlapping them.
key_points: Networks can represent more features than they have dimensions by storing them in overlapping 'superposition.'
This happens when features are sparse — rarely active at the same time — so collisions are tolerable.
Superposition explains 'polysemantic' neurons that respond to several unrelated concepts.
Studied in tiny, controllable toy models where the phenomenon can be observed cleanly.
content_html: Nelson Elhage, Tristan Hume, and colleagues at Anthropic studied a puzzle in interpretability: why individual neurons so often seem to mean several things at once. Their answer is superposition — a network squeezing more features into a layer than it has neurons by storing them in overlapping combinations. Using deliberately tiny "toy" models they can fully analyze, they show exactly when and how this packing happens, giving a clean account of an effect that complicates reading real networks.
extra_html:
How it works

If a layer has, say, 5 neurons, you might expect it to track only 5 things. But if features are sparse — each one active only occasionally — the model can afford to overlap them, assigning each feature a direction even when directions outnumber neurons. Most of the time only a few are active, so the overlaps rarely interfere. The toy models reveal structure in how features get arranged and when the network chooses to superpose versus give a feature its own dedicated direction.

Why it matters

Superposition helps explain why staring at one neuron rarely yields a clean story: a single neuron can participate in many overlapping features at once. That has direct consequences for interpretability and safety, because understanding a model means untangling these overlaps rather than reading neurons one by one. The work motivated later efforts to find the "true" features hidden in superposition, and it remains a key conceptual tool for anyone trying to make sense of model internals.

flashcards.prompt: What is superposition in a neural network?
flashcards.back_html: A network representing more features than it has neurons by storing them in overlapping combinations, giving each feature a direction even when directions outnumber neurons.

flashcards.prompt: What condition lets a network tolerate packing features in superposition?

choices.text: Features are sparse — rarely active at the same time, so collisions are rare
Features are always active together, averaging out noise
The network has more neurons than features

flashcards.explanation_html: When features are sparse, only a few are active at once, so the overlaps rarely interfere — making the packing tolerable.

flashcards.prompt: How does superposition explain polysemantic neurons?
flashcards.back_html: A single neuron can participate in many overlapping features at once, so it appears to respond to several unrelated concepts.
